extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, and USPTO examiners (patent attorneys/agents and policy-makers interested in interview practice)
extracted.subtask_short: examiner interview practice in patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical evaluation of USPTO examiner interview practice: rules (MPEP §713), who may request/attend, timing and pilot programs, best practices for running interviews, recordation requirements, incentives, and recommended reforms to compact prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Basics (MPEP §713)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews are governed by MPEP 713 and may occur in person, via telephone, video conference, electronic mail, or electronic instant message using USPTO tools; internet email/instant messages/video conferences are not secure and require applicant authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical interviews are ~30 minutes; examiners receive 60 minutes of non-production credit (30 min prep + 30 min interview). Applicants may bring demonstrations/exhibits (not generally admitted into the record unless complying with 37 CFR 1.91). An agenda is not required but is typically requested and should include references, claims, specific rejections, and any proposed amendments or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: Right to Interview After First Office Action
rubrics_metrics.description: After the issuance of a first Office Action the patent examiner must grant an interview if requested by the applicant as a matter of right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most interviews occur after the first Office Action to allow discussion of rejections and prior art. Examiners are encouraged to have interviews whenever they would resolve issues and advance prosecution. Interviews are typically scheduled 1–4 weeks in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: Restrictions and Examiner Discretion (Final, Appeal, Issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews are generally not permitted before the first Office Action or after submission of an appeal brief or after a notice of allowance; after a final rejection the examiner has discretion to grant an interview; interviews after an application is sent to issue are generally not permitted except with Technology Center Director approval under extraordinary circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a final, interviews should meaningfully advance prosecution (not merely repeat prior arguments). Interviews that would require more than nominal reconsideration or a new search may be denied. See MPEP §§ 713.09–713.10; 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Programs Allowing Non-Standard Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain programs permit interviews outside normal timing: prioritized examination, Full First Action Interview Pilot Program (FAIPP), and After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP 2.0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAIPP and prioritized examination allow interviews before the first Office Action; AFCP 2.0 enables interviews after a final rejection with extra examiner time for searching/consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who May Request an Interview (Applicant-Initiated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally only the applicant or the attorney/agent of record can request an interview; a party with mere inspection rights cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may request interviews via PTOL-413A, the USPTO Automated Interview Request (AIR) system, or by calling the examiner. Registered practitioners not of record may act if authorized under 37 CFR 1.34 (representative capacity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who May Request an Interview (Examiner-Initiated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners can initiate interviews, but only an examiner with GS-12 or higher and negotiation authority normally may do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner-initiated interviews are often used when the case is close to allowance and typically involve proposed amendments that would lead to allowance. Examiner-initiated interviews are usually fewer per application than applicant-initiated ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who May Participate in an Interview
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants usually include the prosecuting registered patent attorney/agent, the examining patent examiner (working examiner), and the examiner's supervisor (when appropriate); inventors/applicants may attend for technical explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a junior examiner (without signatory/negotiation authority) participates, the supervisor should also participate to reach authoritative agreements. Unregistered or suspended practitioners are barred from conducting interviews unless they are an inventor or applicant in the application. Inventors should be cautioned about making statements that could create estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Request Authority and Binding Parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO normally will not grant an interview unless the requesting party has the ability to bind the principal concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner lacks signatory authority, include a signatory or supervisor. Applicants should ensure their representative has proper authorization (e.g., via PTOL-413A or PTO/SB/84).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Best Practices (Preparation and Conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews should be collaborative to advance prosecution and resolve issues; both parties should prepare agendas, proposed amendments, fallback positions, and be ready to explain rationales for positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants typically provide a written agenda and proposed amendments before the interview; examiners prepare by evaluating claims and prior art. During the interview, parties should aim to resolve outstanding issues and, if an agreement is reached, be able to bind their respective parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordation and Interview Summaries (MPEP §713.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral discussions must be summarized in writing to conform with 37 C.F.R. 1.2; the interview summary should identify claims discussed, specific prior art discussed, and whether an agreement was reached with description of its nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both examiner and applicant must draft interview summaries (the applicant need not write a separate summary if the examiner indicates it's unnecessary). Summaries are typically brief; applicants often prefer minimal summaries to limit prosecution history estoppel. No agreements not on the written record will be recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and Authorization for Unsecured Communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet email, instant messages, or video conferences are not secure and require written or oral authorization from the applicant acknowledging the insecurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorization can be given through EFS-Web (SB/0439), central fax, U.S. Postal Service, or a USPTO customer service window (email does not constitute authorization under USPTO policy). See MPEP §713.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Interview Request (AIR) Tool Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIR tool allows applicants to request an interview, propose dates (between 5 and 35 days after submission), and include optional agenda/topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants supply application number, type of interview (in-person/telephonic/video), representative registration number, proposed time/date and two alternatives, and optionally an agenda. Useful when applicants cannot reach an examiner by phone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology Center Interview Specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Technology Center has at least one interview specialist who are subject-matter experts on interview practice and policy and can assist with technical/technology issues and WebEx/technical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview specialists also help train examiners on conducting interviews and using video interview technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Incentives and Count System for Interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO gives 'non-production time' credit for substantive applicant-initiated and examiner-initiated interviews; examiners receive one hour of non-production credit for interview practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-hour credit typically covers 30 minutes of preparation and 30 minutes of interview time. The PTO increased interview hours and staff involvement since 2008; additional incentives (beyond the one-hour count) were not standard at time of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIPP (Full First Action Interview Pilot Program) Eligibility Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To enroll in FAIPP the application must meet six requirements: (1) not a reissue, provisional, or national stage of an international application; (2) ≤3 independent claims and ≤20 total claims; (3) no multiple dependent claims; (4) single invention and agreement to election without traverse if Office finds multiple inventions; (5) request filed electronically at least one day before first Office Action on the merits appears in PAIR; (6) applicant agrees not to request refunds of search/excess claim fees after mailing of the pre-interview communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under FAIPP the applicant receives a condensed pre-interview communication (search results and proposed rejections), schedules an interview within 30 days, and submits proposed amendments/arguments. The substance of the interview must be made of record and a complete written statement regarding merits is made of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIPP Possible Outcomes and Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAIPP outlines three outcomes: (1) agreement reached and claims in condition for allowance (examiner completes PTOL-413 and issues Notice of Allowance); (2) no agreement and examiner issues a First Action Interview Office Action listing unresolved/maintained/new rejections (considered the first Office Action on merits); (3) no agreement and applicant converts proposed amendment into a reply under 37 CFR 1.111(b) and waives receipt of First Action Interview Office Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must respond to a First Action Interview Office Action within two months (extendable). FAIPP showed higher first-action allowance rates (~29% FAIPP vs ~14% for comparable new non-continuing applications) in cited data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data Metrics for Evaluating Interview Effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Key empirical metrics: Office Action to Grant Ratio (OGR), Office Action to Abandonment Ratio (OAR), number of Office Actions to final disposition (allowance or abandonment), issued vs abandoned applications, and examiner-paired average disposition rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dataset in study: 1,008,989 applications with ≥1 interview that issued, 146,851 with ≥1 interview that were abandoned. Data were segmented by Technology Center and by whether interviews were applicant-initiated (PTOL-413A) or examiner-initiated (PTOL-413B), and tracked exact number of interviews per application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant vs Examiner Initiation Tracking (PTOL Forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant-initiated interviews are tracked via PTOL-413A forms; examiner-initiated interviews via PTOL-413B forms; scheduling without PTOL forms is captured in total interviews counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study distinguishes between total interviews and those recorded by PTOL forms to determine the number of applicant- or examiner-initiated interviews before allowance or abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on Interview Outcomes and Subsequent Searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an agreement is reached during the interview, the examiner will conduct a final update and interference search which could identify prior art negating the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No oral agreement is binding unless placed in the written record; the final search can change allowance prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to Improve Interview Practice: Require Proposed Claim Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Require both applicants and examiners to bring concrete proposed claim language to interviews to focus discussions and provide starting points for resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys show dissatisfaction with 'ways to overcome the rejection'—requiring draft claim language from both sides would help clarify solutions and how the examiner interprets claims/prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to Improve Interview Practice: More Detailed Interview Summaries / Recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a more detailed written interview summary (independent examiner draft, applicant may respond) or include audio/video recordings in the file to improve public record and aid later claim construction/estoppel analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed summaries would improve transparency and allow courts/competitors to see rationale for amendments; applicants currently often prefer brief, opaque summaries to limit estoppel. Proposal examples include requiring a ~500-word examiner summary and an examiner-drafted claim addressing a rejection to get extra non-production credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to Improve Interview Practice: Tie Interviews to Examiner Promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie competency and participation in interview practice to examiner promotions by requiring a specific number of interviews for advancement to the next GS level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is suggested as an incentive to ensure examiners engage meaningfully in interview practice if the PTO views interviews as valuable to compact prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to Improve Interview Practice: Increase Examiner Non-Production Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase non-production time allotment for interview practice (e.g., from one hour to two hours) to reflect actual preparation and documentation needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing allotted time would allow examiners to better review prior art and applicant arguments, and could be paired with requirements for more detailed interview summaries or drafting claims to overcome rejections; extra time could be conditioned on producing more substantive outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution Rationale: Interviews Compact Prosecution (Bridge Misunderstandings & Signal Value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal rationales for why interviews reduce the number of Office Actions: (1) bridging misunderstandings/miscommunications between examiner and applicant via real-time discussion and inventor demonstrations; (2) interviews act as a signal that the application is valuable to the applicant, prompting examiner accommodation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: applications with interviews require dramatically fewer Office Actions to reach final disposition compared to examiner average; interviews can lower prosecution cost/time and reduce unnecessary cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIPP Statistical Outcomes and Effectiveness Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: FAIPP outcomes: possible first action allowance and higher first-action allowance rates were observed (e.g., 29% first action allowance in FAIPP vs ~14% for new, non-continuing apps; earlier pilots reported ~33.5%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAIPP shows a higher likelihood of disposition in fewer actions; studies cited show FAIPP applications have higher allowance rates and, in one dataset, 94% of FAIPP applications were allowed compared to 76% overall for applications (citation dependent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope Limitations: Exclusions and Application Types
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain application types are excluded from interview-related datasets and pilots (e.g., design patents in this dataset; FAIPP excludes reissue/provisional/national stage PCT entries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study removed Technology Center 2900 (design patents) to focus on utility patents. Pilot programs have their own eligibility restrictions to ensure program objectives.
